summary.text: The block \([2,4,2,4,2]\), beginning at index \(3\), comes from the consecutive primes \(5,7,11,13,17,19\). Any occurrence would give primes at \(P,P+2,P+6,P+8,P+12,P+14\); the five offsets \(0,2,6,8,14\) cover every residue modulo \(5\), forcing \(P=5\) (the only apparent alternative \(P=3\) makes \(P+6=9\)), so the block occurs only at its original index.

full_proof.text:
Let \(p_1=2,p_2=3,p_3=5,\ldots\) denote the primes in increasing order, and let
\[
a(n)=p_{n+1}-p_n\qquad(n\ge 1).
\]
The statement to be disproved says that, for every \(n>2\) and every \(m\ge 0\), the block
\[
(a(n),a(n+1),\ldots,a(n+m))
\]
occurs at infinitely many starting indices.

We exhibit a block beginning at the allowed index \(n=3\) which in fact has only one occurrence.

The first eight primes are
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(3)&=7-5=2,\\
a(4)&=11-7=4,\\
a(5)&=13-11=2,\\
a(6)&=17-13=4,\\
a(7)&=19-17=2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the five-term block beginning at index \(3\) is
\[
(a(3),a(4),a(5),a(6),a(7))=(2,4,2,4,2). \tag{1}
\]
(The displayed initial list of primes is checked directly: each listed number is prime by testing possible prime divisors up to its square root, and every intervening integer greater than \(3\) is visibly divisible by \(2\), \(3\), or \(5\).)

We now prove that (1) cannot begin anywhere else. Suppose first that \(k\ge 1\) and
\[
(a(k),a(k+1),a(k+2),a(k+3),a(k+4))=(2,4,2,4,2). \tag{2}
\]
Put
\[
P=p_k.
\]
Because the entries of (2) are the successive differences between consecutive primes, adding the gaps cumulatively gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_{k+1}&=P+2,\\
p_{k+2}&=P+2+4=P+6,\\
p_{k+3}&=P+2+4+2=P+8,\\
p_{k+4}&=P+2+4+2+4=P+12,\\
p_{k+5}&=P+2+4+2+4+2=P+14.
\end{aligned} \tag{3}
\]
In particular, all of
\[
P,\quad P+2,\quad P+6,\quad P+8,\quad P+14 \tag{4}
\]
are prime. We will not even need the additional prime \(P+12\).

Consider \(P\) modulo \(5\). The five offsets
\[
0,2,6,8,14
\]
have residues
\[
0,2,1,3,4 \pmod 5,
\]
respectively. They therefore cover every residue modulo \(5\). More explicitly, a case split on the residue of \(P\) gives the following:

* If \(P\equiv0\pmod5\), then \(5\mid P\). Since \(P\) is prime, this forces \(P=5\).

* If \(P\equiv1\pmod5\), then \(P+14\equiv0\pmod5\). But \(P\) is a prime and hence \(P\ge2\), so \(P+14>5\). Thus \(P+14\) is a multiple of \(5\) greater than \(5\), contradicting its primality.

* If \(P\equiv2\pmod5\), then \(P+8\equiv0\pmod5\). Again \(P+8>5\), so it cannot be prime, contrary to (4).

* If \(P\equiv3\pmod5\), then \(P+2\equiv0\pmod5\). Since \(P+2\) is prime, it must equal \(5\), and hence \(P=3\). But then \(P+6=9\), which is composite, again contradicting (4).

* If \(P\equiv4\pmod5\), then \(P+6\equiv0\pmod5\), and \(P+6>5\); hence \(P+6\) is composite, another contradiction.

The only surviving possibility is therefore
\[
P=5. \tag{5}
\]
Since \(P=p_k\) and \(5\\) is the third prime, (5) implies \(k=3\). The strict increase of the prime sequence ensures that no other index can also have prime value \(5\).

If starting indices are taken to include \(k=0\) by extending the sequence with the convention \(a(0)=0\), that case cannot supply another occurrence either: a five-term block beginning at \(0\) has first entry \(0\), whereas the block in (1) has first entry \(2\). Thus among all nonnegative starting indices, every occurrence of the block (1) starts at \(k=3\). Conversely, (1) shows that it really does occur there. Hence its set of starting indices is exactly the singleton
\[
\{3\}.
\]

Finally, choose \(n=3\) and \(m=4\) in the proposed assertion. These values satisfy \(n>2\) and \(m\ge0\), and the relevant block \(a(n),\ldots,a(n+m)\) is precisely the five-term block (1). Its occurrence set is the finite set \(\{3\}\), not an infinite set. Therefore the conjecture is false.
